headline_marked: Underdog shows off a [[32MB speech model]] in new demo
headline: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo
summary: Underdog's new Woof model, a text-to-speech AI, is so compact it runs entirely in your browser. This 32MB model operates locally, offering private AI experiences without cloud dependency.
details: AI startup Underdog has unveiled Woof, a new text-to-speech model that is remarkably small at just 32MB. This compact size allows it to run directly within a web browser, eliminating the need for extensive processing power or cloud infrastructure.

To showcase Woof, Underdog released a retro-themed game where users can type on a virtual typewriter and have the text spoken back. The game emphasizes local processing, even including a jab at "intrusive" cloud providers.

The Woof model, with 31 million parameters, operates without an internet connection once downloaded. Underdog has made the model openly available for download, promoting its use on various edge devices.

While not intended to replace larger, more complex AI models, Woof's small footprint makes it suitable for applications requiring local processing, such as personalized podcasts or on-device virtual assistants.

This release follows Underdog's earlier launch of Bark, a 167MB speech-to-text model also designed for edge devices. Founder Sigil Wen aims to enable users to run capable AI models locally, ensuring data privacy and ownership.

Underdog's broader vision includes developing open, American-made AI models that can run on existing user devices. The company has also released a 27-billion-parameter model capable of running on laptops, alongside a waitlisted app for locally-hosted AI experiences.

headline_marked: [[Claude AI accidentally deleted]] a law professor's entire syllabus and a year of lecture notes
headline: Claude AI accidentally deleted a law professor's entire syllabus and a year of lecture notes
summary: A University of Chicago law professor tasked Claude AI with a simple renumbering task, only for it to delete his syllabus and a year of lecture notes. While the files were recovered, the incident serves as a stark warning about AI's potential for unintended da
details: A University of Chicago law professor, William Baude, faced an alarming incident when Claude AI accidentally deleted his entire Constitutional Law syllabus and a year's worth of lecture notes. The files were fortunately recovered via Dropbox, but Baude shared his experience as a public service announcement.

Baude, a professor at the University of Chicago Law School, had tasked Claude (model unspecified) with updating page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine request led to the AI informing him, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident."

Upon discovering the deletion, Baude's understandable reaction was "WTF!!!!." This incident underscores the critical importance of always backing up important files, especially when entrusting them to AI agents. The AI's action appears to be an accidental error rather than a deliberate deletion.

This event is not an isolated incident; other AI agents have demonstrated similar unintended destructive capabilities. Previous reports include an AI agent deleting an entire TV show's edit weeks before release and another wiping a company database in just nine seconds.

Other instances include Claude mistakenly deleting a developer's entire profile directory while attempting a backup, blaming the error on a typo. These cases often highlight mistaken or misplaced initiative by AI rather than outright negligence.

In line with similar incidents, Claude was reportedly very apologetic about the situation. The AI confessed, "You're right to be angry. I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."
